packages.name: triage-host
packages.description: Summarize what a host does, how it is built, how it signs users in, and where to look first.
packages.author: Plonix contributors
about: Gives an agent a repeatable way to size up a host: what it serves, how it is built, how it signs users in, and which requests deserve a first look.
The agent reads your captured traffic, the technologies Plonix detected and the host's map. It does not send anything.
Use it when you land on a new target and want a briefing before you start digging.

packages.name: explain-request
packages.description: Walk through one captured request and its response in plain language, including tokens and encoded values.
packages.author: Plonix contributors
about: Walks an agent through one captured request and its response: what the call is for, what each header, cookie and parameter does, and anything that looks unusual.
Give it a request id. The agent reads that exchange and the Lens insights Plonix spotted in it, and answers in plain language.
Good for unfamiliar APIs, tokens you do not recognise and long minified responses.

packages.name: review-sign-in
packages.description: Find the sign-in, sign-out and session requests and describe how the application keeps users signed in.
packages.author: Plonix contributors
about: Has an agent follow how a site signs users in: the requests involved, where tokens and cookies are set, and what is worth testing next.
It reads captured traffic only. It does not try credentials or replay anything.
Run it after you have signed in to the target once in the browser behind Plonix.

packages.name: check-scope
packages.description: Go through scope suggestions and recommend which domains belong to the target, with the evidence for each.
packages.author: Plonix contributors
about: Goes through the domains Plonix suggests for scope and recommends which belong to the target, with a line of evidence for each.

Accept means it is the target's own (shared cookies, its certificate, calls made by its pages). Keep out means a third-party service such as analytics or a CDN. Ask the owner means the evidence is thin.
The agent only reads. You decide in the Scope screen.

packages.name: draft-finding
packages.description: Turn an observed issue into a clear, reproducible finding write-up to review and record in Plonix.
packages.author: Plonix contributors
about: Helps an agent turn something you found into a clear write-up: a title, the steps to reproduce, the evidence from your traffic, the impact and a suggested fix.
It reads the requests and findings you point it at and drafts text for you to review. Agents are read-only, so you record the finding yourself.
Use it when you want a first draft you can tidy up.

packages.name: api-inventory
packages.description: List every API operation seen on a host with its parameters, authentication and data returned.
packages.author: Plonix contributors
about: Builds an inventory of a target's API from what you have captured: endpoints, methods, parameters, authentication and how responses are shaped.
The agent reads your traffic and the site map. It does not probe the API.
Handy before you test, and for handing a clear picture of an API to a teammate.

packages.name: api-kit
packages.description: Everything for testing an API: the API inventory skill, filters for leaked secrets and debug output, and admin console detection.
packages.author: Plonix contributors
about: A starter set for working on APIs. It installs the API inventory skill, the leaks filter pack and the admin panels rule pack together.
Removing the bundle removes the parts it installed. Every part is checked before anything is added.
Choose it if API testing is most of what you do.

packages.name: graphql-explorer
packages.description: A GraphQL tab: every operation seen in traffic, grouped by type, with its variables and the requests that used it.
packages.author: Plonix contributors
about: A planned extension that adds a GraphQL tab: browse a schema, see queries in a readable form and build requests from them.
Extensions that run code need the sandboxed extension runtime, which is not in this version of Plonix yet. It is listed so you can see what is coming and what it would be allowed to do.
It cannot be installed yet.

packages.name: web-servers
packages.description: Common HTTP servers and application servers, from response headers.
packages.author: Plonix contributors
about: Recognises web servers, proxies and application servers from the headers and markers they leave: nginx, Apache, IIS, Caddy, Envoy, Traefik, HAProxy, Gunicorn, Tomcat, Kestrel and more.
Rule packs are data, not code. They only match on captured traffic and show their findings in the Map and the Lens.
Built in.

packages.name: frameworks
packages.description: Server-side languages and web frameworks, from headers, cookies and markup.
packages.author: Plonix contributors
about: Recognises web frameworks and libraries from cookies, headers, paths and page markers, such as Rails, Django, Laravel, Express, Next.js and Spring.
Rule packs are data, not code. They only match on captured traffic.
Built in. Knowing the framework tells you what to try and what to skip.

packages.name: cms
packages.description: Content management systems and e-commerce platforms.
packages.author: Plonix contributors
about: Recognises content management and commerce platforms: WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, Ghost, Magento, Shopify, WooCommerce, Strapi and similar.
Rule packs are data, not code. They only match on captured traffic.
Built in. Knowing the platform tells you where to look first.

packages.name: edge
packages.description: CDNs, WAFs, caches and hosting platforms in front of the application.
packages.author: Plonix contributors
about: Recognises the CDNs, firewalls and hosting platforms in front of a site, from the headers, cookies and markers they add: Cloudflare, Fastly, Akamai, CloudFront, Vercel, Netlify and more.
Rule packs are data, not code. They only match on captured traffic.
Built in. Helps you tell what is the target and what is the layer in front of it.

packages.name: api-surface
packages.description: API styles, API documentation and identity endpoints worth a closer look.
packages.author: Plonix contributors
about: Recognises API styles and sign-in systems from captured traffic: GraphQL, OpenAPI docs, gRPC-Web, JSON-RPC, SOAP, OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect, Keycloak, Auth0, Okta and JSON Web Tokens.
Rule packs are data, not code. They only match on captured traffic.
Built in. Shows where a target keeps its API and how it signs users in.

packages.name: admin-panels
packages.description: DevOps tools and admin consoles that are often exposed by mistake.
packages.author: Plonix contributors
about: Spots admin and management consoles from what their pages say and where they live: Jenkins, GitLab, Grafana, Kibana, Prometheus, phpMyAdmin, Kubernetes Dashboard and more.
Rule packs are data, not code. They only match on captured traffic and never request anything.
Not built in. Add it when you want admin interfaces called out.

packages.name: common
packages.description: Everyday Traffic filters: API calls, auth flows, admin areas, writes, and tracker noise to hide.
packages.author: Plonix contributors
about: Named filters for the questions you ask most: API calls, GraphQL, sign-in traffic, admin paths, writes, uploads, redirects, failures, denied requests, API docs, files, and a filter that hides trackers.
Use them in the search box as is:auth or -is:trackers, or pick them from the Filter button. They only narrow what you see.
Built in.

packages.name: leaks
packages.description: Find traffic that leaks secrets, stack traces or debug output.
packages.author: Plonix contributors
about: Filters that find traffic likely to expose something sensitive: AWS keys, private keys, JSON Web Tokens, stack traces, SQL errors, debug pages, source maps and internal IP addresses.
Use them as is:aws-keys and similar. They only narrow what you see and change nothing.
Add it when you review a target for sensitive data exposure.

packages.name: starter-lists
packages.description: The payload lists that ship with Plonix, for the Bench.
packages.author: Plonix contributors
about: The lists Plonix starts with for Bench payload runs: digits and number ranges, common parameter and path names, usernames, HTTP methods, content types, user agents and a small set of benign input probes.
Choose one in the Bench Run panel as a built-in list, or feed it a position from the command line with `--list builtin:<id>`.
Built in, so it is always available even offline.

packages.name: extra-wordlists
packages.description: More starting-point lists for the Bench: id formats, ports, and common API paths.
packages.author: Plonix contributors
about: Extra payload lists for the Bench beyond the built-in starters: identifier shapes to try where a number is expected, common ports, and API endpoints worth probing.
Install it from the Market, then pick its lists in the Bench Run panel like any other.
Data only: a list supplies values you choose to send, through the usual scope-gated send path.

packages.name: hackerone
packages.description: Brings in the HackerOne programs you can hack on, with each program's scope and rules.
packages.author: Plonix contributors
about: Connect your HackerOne account once with an API token. The Programs screen then lists every program you can work on, and bringing one in sets this project's scope from the program's structured scope: in-scope assets are accepted, listed exclusions are rejected.

Plonix also reads the program's policy for its rules of engagement: a request rate, headers to add to every request, and whether automated testing or disruptive tests are banned. You review all of it before it applies, and from then on Plonix enforces it on everything it sends.
The token is kept in your Keychain and is only ever sent to api.hackerone.com. AI agents never see it.
Built in, so it is always available.
